title: Children and builders (Berakhot 64a)
hook: the rabbis read banayich, your children, as bonayich, your builders

segments.voice: Yesterday, Y-D-A: yada, to know, the verb for a fact, a friend and a marriage. Your line was to know is to be close. Did you ask your real question? Today, one word read two ways. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

On a living-room rug, a kid is stacking blocks. Red on blue, a yellow one balanced on top, a tower that leans and somehow holds. An adult walks past and sees a mess to tidy before dinner. The kid sees a city. Who's right? The Talmud has an answer, and it hides in a single vowel. Near its close, tractate Berakhot, the tractate of blessings, quotes a verse from Isaiah about children, and a rabbi reads one word of it a second way. Same letters. Different sound. Today the word for children turns into the word for builders.
screen: `A KID, A TOWER OF BLOCKS.` → `A MESS, OR A CITY?` → `ONE WORD, READ TWICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, from Isaiah, as the old Jewish Publication Society translation has it: "And all thy children shall be taught of the LORD; And great shall be the peace of thy children." Turn it four ways. First, the word. Thy children, in Hebrew, is banayich. Ben, a son, a child, with the ending that means yours. Second, the move. In Berakhot, Rabbi Elazar, in the name of Rabbi Chanina, says that students of the wise increase peace in the world, and he quotes this verse. Then he adds: don't read banayich, your children. Read bonayich, your builders. Write the word without its vowel marks, the way it stands in a scroll, and the two look alike. Only the sound changes. Third, what kind of move that is. The rabbis call it al tikri, don't read. It doesn't erase the plain meaning. Isaiah still says children. The second reading stands beside the first, like a harmony line sung over a melody. So the verse now says two things at once: your children will be taught, and your builders will have great peace. Fourth, who the builders are. In the passage, they're the ones who learn. A child taught today is already laying stones for a peace that hasn't been built yet. Which brings us back to the rug. The adult sees a mess before dinner. The Talmud, reading Isaiah, sees a builder at work. The tower leans. The child is learning how a thing holds. And according to Berakhot, that learning is how peace gets built.
screen: `BANAYICH: YOUR CHILDREN.` · `READ IT BONAYICH: YOUR BUILDERS.` · `AL TIKRI: A SECOND READING BESIDE.` · `THE LEARNERS BUILD THE PEACE.` · then, large: `בניך`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage a child. Settle, and breathe. Bring one child to mind: your own, a niece, a student, a kid down the street. If no child comes, bring the child you once were. Picture them building something: a tower, a drawing, a question they keep asking. See the thing they made, not the mess around it. Now find one sentence of encouragement you could say to them, about the building, not about being good. Hold it until it sounds like you. If you pray, you can hold their name in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Children and builders. Banayich and bonayich: one set of letters in Isaiah, read two ways in the Talmud, so that the children are the builders. Today's word.
Your line: children are builders. Today, say your sentence to that child, or to a younger person you see, and name one thing they made. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: The passage from the end of tractate Berakhot, with its reading of banayich as bonayich, is printed in some prayer books and is quoted at some celebrations of learning, such as the completion of a tractate.

fork.setup: you're a rabbi reading Isaiah: "great shall be the peace of thy children." the word for children catches your eye. what do you do?
options: read the same letters a second way: your builders.
fork.reveal: don't read banayich, read bonayich. the children are the builders, and the learners build the peace.

original.note: Hebrew, without vowel marks: the same letters read as your children or your builders.

trapdoor: what you thought: children are the ones adults build.
what it means: the Talmud reads Isaiah's word for your children as your builders.
what a scholar hears: al tikri, a rabbinic reading that changes the vowels and keeps the letters.

notes: Editor: the Isaiah verse is quoted near the close of Berakhot, not as its last line (Psalms verses follow), so the hook now says 'near its close'; softened howItsDone 'often quoted' to 'quoted at some'.
Confirm JPS 1917 wording and line capitalization of Isaiah 54:13.

Berakhot 64a paraphrased: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina; students of the wise increase peace; al tikri banayich ela bonayich. Confirm attribution and that the tractate closes with this passage ('closes with').
howItsDone says the passage is 'printed in some prayer books' (e.g. after Ein Keloheinu, and in the Kaddish d'Rabbanan context) and quoted at a siyum; confirm or soften.
Original given unpointed (בניך) on purpose, since the point is the shared consonants; in Isaiah the vowels differ between the two occurrences. Confirm transliteration banayich/bonayich.
Description of al tikri as not erasing the plain meaning is a common traditional understanding; a Keeper may refine.
